history.heading: Amazigh kingdoms and Islamic dynasties
paragraphs: Morocco has been inhabited for hundreds of thousands of years; the oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, about 300,000 years old, were found at Jebel Irhoud. Amazigh (Berber) peoples formed kingdoms such as Mauretania, which became a Roman province; Volubilis was an important Roman city.

Arab armies brought Islam in the late 7th century. The Idrisid dynasty, founded in 788, established Fez, home to al-Qarawiyyin, one of the oldest universities in the world. Amazigh dynasties, the Almoravids and Almohads, built empires stretching into Spain, and Marrakesh became a great capital.

history.heading: Saadians and Alaouites
paragraphs: The Saadian dynasty defeated Portugal at the Battle of the Three Kings in 1578. The Alaouite dynasty, which still rules, took power in the 1660s. Morocco remained independent of the Ottoman Empire and was one of the first states to recognise the United States, in 1777.

history.heading: Protectorate and independence
paragraphs: In 1912 Morocco became a French protectorate, with Spain controlling the north and south. The Rif War against Spain in the 1920s, led by Abd el-Krim, was a major anti-colonial struggle. Morocco regained independence in 1956 under Sultan Mohammed V, who became king.

King Hassan II ruled from 1961 to 1999, a period of repression known as the "Years of Lead". In 1975 he organised the Green March into Western Sahara. Mohammed VI succeeded him in 1999. After the 2011 Arab Spring protests, a new constitution gave parliament more powers. Morocco normalised relations with Israel in 2020, and an earthquake in the Atlas Mountains killed nearly 3,000 people in 2023.

culture.heading: Peoples and languages
paragraphs: Arabic and Tamazight (Amazigh) are official languages; Moroccan Arabic (Darija) is spoken in daily life, and French is widely used in business and education. Almost all Moroccans are Sunni Muslim, and there is a historic Jewish community.
The medinas of Fez and Marrakesh are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, famous for their souks, riads and craftsmanship in zellige tiles, leather and carpets.

culture.heading: Food, music and sport
paragraphs: Moroccan cuisine includes tagine, couscous, pastilla, harira soup and mint tea, an essential symbol of hospitality. Gnawa music, with spiritual African roots, is recognised by UNESCO.
Football is a passion; Morocco became the first African and Arab team to reach the World Cup semi-finals in 2022, and will co-host the 2030 World Cup with Spain and Portugal.

politics.heading: Constitutional monarchy
paragraphs: Morocco is a constitutional monarchy in which the king holds broad powers over religion, the military, foreign policy and key appointments. The prime minister is appointed from the party that wins the most seats in parliament. In 2025 youth-led "Gen Z 212" protests demanded better healthcare and education.

politics.heading: Western Sahara
paragraphs: Morocco controls most of Western Sahara, which it considers its southern provinces, while the Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks independence. Morocco's autonomy plan has gained support from the United States, France, Spain and others, and in 2025 a UN Security Council resolution endorsed it as a basis for negotiations.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Morocco holds over 70 percent of the world's phosphate reserves, vital for fertilisers, through the state company OCP. It has become a major car manufacturer (Renault and Stellantis plants) and exporter of aeronautics components, textiles and agricultural products.
Tourism is a key sector. Morocco is a leader in renewable energy, with the large Noor solar complex. Challenges include youth unemployment, rural poverty, and drought. The currency is the dirham.
